lessons.title: Signed linear momentum
lessons.summary: Use one positive direction, calculate the momentum of each particle and combine signed contributions on a straight line.
lessons.objective: Find momentum, mass or signed velocity using p = mv and solve simple total-momentum problems.
lessons.before: Recall the distinction between velocity and speed, and convert grams to kilograms.
lessons.method:
1. Choose one direction as positive.
  2. Multiply the mass in kilograms by the signed velocity.
  3. Add components along the chosen line and interpret the sign.
mistakes: Speed gives a magnitude. Velocity specifies a direction as well.
Momentum inherits the sign of the velocity.
Zero total can result from two non-zero contributions that cancel.
lessons.ideas:
\(p=mv\). A positive mass never changes the sign: the momentum points in the same physical direction as the velocity.

\(1000\,\mathrm g=1\,\mathrm{kg}\). The usual momentum unit is \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\(v=\frac{p}{m}\). If \(v\ne0\), \(m=\frac{p}{v}\). A stationary particle has zero momentum for every positive mass.

For two particles on one line, \(P=m_Av_A+m_Bv_B\). Use one positive direction for both.

Zero total means \(m_Av_A=-m_Bv_B\). With nonzero values, the directions are opposite and the magnitudes agree.

A sign reversal changes the description rather than the motion. State the convention so the result can be interpreted.

examples.title: Find the signed momentum of one particle
examples.question:
A particle has mass \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{kg}\) and moves to the left at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give its signed momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
The mass is already in kilograms and the signed velocity is \(-4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Apply \(p=mv\). The result is \(-10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the signed momentum of one particle
examples.question:
A particle has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and is at rest.

Take rightward as positive.

Give its signed momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
The mass is already in kilograms and the signed velocity is \(0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Apply \(p=mv\). The result is \(0\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the signed momentum of one particle
examples.question:
A particle has mass \(480\,\mathrm g\) and moves to the left at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give its signed momentum in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Convert \(480\,\mathrm g\) to \(\frac{12}{25}\,\mathrm{kg}\) before multiplying.

Apply \(p=mv\). The result is \(- \frac{12}{5}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Recover positive mass from signed data
examples.question:
Take rightward as positive.

A particle moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and its signed momentum is \(-12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its mass in kilograms.
examples.solution:
Use the signed velocity \(-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its sign is the same as the given momentum.

\(m=\frac{-12}{-3}=4\), which is positive.

lessons.title: Direct collisions and missing velocities
lessons.summary: Set up a signed momentum equation before and after direct impact, then recover missing velocities or a mass from the stated data.
lessons.objective: Apply conservation of linear momentum to direct impacts with complete data.
lessons.before: Recall signed linear momentum and how to solve a linear equation.
lessons.method:
1. Choose the pair of particles and a positive direction.
  2. Write their totals immediately before and after contact.
  3. Use the extra condition if two quantities are unknown, then check signs and ordering.
mistakes: Use the same positive direction throughout.
Give the requested speed or signed velocity.
One momentum equation does not determine two independent unknown velocities.
lessons.ideas:
\(m_Au_A+m_Bu_B=m_Av_A+m_Bv_B\), with \(u\) just before, \(v\) just after.

Substitute the known final contribution, then subtract it from the previously calculated total.

After finding a negative signed velocity, state the non-negative speed with the direction if the question requests both.

Equate the known total to the side which has the unknown initial velocity.

\(m_A(u_A-v_A)=m_B(v_B-u_B)\). Check that the calculated mass is positive.

Write the relation using signed velocities. If the condition is a ratio of speeds, use the stated directions to remove the absolute values.

examples.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest. Immediately after impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{4}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(5)+(3)(0)=(3)v+(2)(\frac{4}{5})\]

Hence \(v=\frac{14}{5}\). The particle moves to the right at \(\frac{14}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest. Immediately after impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{12}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(4)(6)+(3)(0)=(3)v+(4)(\frac{12}{7})\]

Hence \(v=\frac{40}{7}\). The particle moves to the right at \(\frac{40}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest. Immediately after impact, B moves to the right at \(\frac{16}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the speed of A in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and select its direction.
examples.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(10\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(5)+(5)(0)=(2)v+(5)(\frac{16}{7})\]

Hence \(v=- \frac{5}{7}\). The particle moves to the left at \(\frac{5}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the missing velocity after impact
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after impact, A is at rest.

Give the signed velocity of B in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Use the same positive direction on both sides. Before impact, the total is \(6\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3)(4)+(2)(-3)=(2)v+(3)(0)\]

Hence \(v=3\). The particle moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

lessons.title: Coalescence and common velocity
lessons.summary: Combine the masses when two particles stick, calculate their shared velocity and work backwards from a stated common motion.
lessons.objective: Use conservation of momentum to find common or initial velocities and unknown masses after a direct impact where bodies coalesce.
lessons.before: Recall the before and after equation for direct impact, with signed velocities along one line.
lessons.method:
1. Write the total momentum before the collision.
  2. Replace the two final terms by the combined mass times their common velocity.
  3. Check the sign and whether the result lies between the two initial velocities.
mistakes: One common velocity applies to both masses.
Add masses, including for opposite directions.
Equal and opposite momenta give a stationary joined pair.
lessons.ideas:
\(m_Au_A+m_Bu_B=(m_A+m_B)v\). The common velocity carries a sign.

The direction of common motion follows the sign of the total initial momentum under the chosen convention.

Set \(m_Au_A+m_Bu_B=0\) if the particles coalesce and stop.

For an unknown initial velocity, subtract the other contribution and divide by the mass of the corresponding particle.

\(m_B(v-u_B)=m_A(u_A-v)\). Check positivity after solving.

When the initial velocities differ, the common velocity is strictly between them. Momentum conservation determines exactly where it lies.

examples.title: Find a shared final velocity
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B is at rest.

Give the signed velocity of the joined pair in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Since the particles stick, their common velocity \(v\) is multiplied by the combined mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\).

\[(3)(5)+(2)(0)=15=5v\]

\(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find a shared final velocity
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of the joined pair in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Since the particles stick, their common velocity \(v\) is multiplied by the combined mass \(7\,\mathrm{kg}\).

\[(4)(6)+(3)(1)=27=7v\]

\(\frac{27}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle moves to the right at \(\frac{27}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find a shared final velocity
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) and B has mass \(7\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of the joined pair in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Since the particles stick, their common velocity \(v\) is multiplied by the combined mass \(11\,\mathrm{kg}\).

\[(4)(3)+(7)(-2)=-2=11v\]

\(- \frac{2}{11}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The particle moves to the left at \(\frac{2}{11}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Determine the mass needed to stop
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive. The particles remain joined after impact.

A has mass \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Afterwards the joined pair is at rest.

Find the mass of B in kilograms.
examples.solution:
Write the final momentum as \((4+m)(0)\).

\[(4)(5)+m(-4)=(4+m)(0)\]

Collecting gives \(m(4)=20\). Therefore \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\).

lessons.title: Approach, separation and compatible collision data
lessons.summary: Read the order of particles, translate speed conditions into signed equations and test whether a collision report respects momentum and separation.
lessons.objective: Check whether stated collision data describe approach and separation and determine both velocities from a second condition.
lessons.before: Recall signed motion, direct impacts and constant-velocity displacement.
lessons.method:
1. Draw the left particle and right particle before comparing velocities.
  2. Check the before and after momentum of the pair.
  3. Use a second condition to find both velocities when necessary.
mistakes: Speed alone does not specify direction.
A momentum match does not settle which particle is moving ahead.
An opening gap requires the final signed velocity on the right to be larger.
lessons.ideas:
If \(v_A>v_B\), the gap closes. This rule also works if both are moving left.

For initial gap \(d>0\) and \(v_A>v_B\), time to contact is \(\frac{d}{v_A-v_B}\).

Check \(v_B-v_A>0\). A zero gap-opening rate alone does not prove that the bodies joined.

Require both an equal total and a positive gap-opening rate if the stated outcome is a separating collision.

When A moves left and B moves right, a positive speed ratio \(k\) gives \(v_B=-kv_A\). Use the momentum equation with this relation.

For known total \(P\), the sign condition for separation forces \(v_A<\frac P{m_A+m_B}\) after substituting the momentum equation.

examples.title: Calculate the rate at which the gap closes
examples.question:
At one instant A is \(3\,\mathrm m\) to the left of B. A moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give the signed closing rate, defined as \(v_A-v_B\), in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Decide what the gap then does if velocities are constant.
examples.solution:
Subtract the right-hand velocity from the left-hand velocity: \((2)-(1)=1\).

The two particles approach.

examples.title: Calculate the rate at which the gap closes
examples.question:
At one instant A is \(4\,\mathrm m\) to the left of B. A moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Take rightward as positive.

Give the signed closing rate, defined as \(v_A-v_B\), in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Decide what the gap then does if velocities are constant.
examples.solution:
Subtract the right-hand velocity from the left-hand velocity: \((-2)-(-5)=3\).

The two particles approach.

examples.title: Test whether the gap closes
examples.question:
A is \(14\,\mathrm m\) to the left of B. A moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves to the left at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at constant velocities.

Take rightward as positive.

Decide whether they meet. If they meet, give the time to contact in seconds.
examples.solution:
The signed rate at which the gap closes is \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The left particle must have a greater signed velocity to make contact.

Divide the starting gap \(14\,\mathrm m\) by the positive closing rate to obtain \(\frac{7}{4}\,\mathrm s\).

examples.title: Compare a collision report with two requirements
examples.question:
Two particles move on the same smooth horizontal line. A is to the left of B immediately before impact. Take rightward as positive.

A and B have masses \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\). Before impact, A moves to the right at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest.

A report describes the immediate state afterwards as follows. A moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Which tests pass: matching total momentum, and an immediate opening of the gap?
examples.solution:
Before and proposed after totals are \(18\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(18\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). They match.

The proposed gap-opening rate is \(-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is not positive.

Momentum remains the same only.

lessons.title: Successive impacts on one line
lessons.summary: Track a changed velocity through two separate direct impacts, use each pair’s momentum and check a possible later contact.
lessons.objective: Apply the momentum equation separately to each direct one-dimensional collision using its declared data.
lessons.before: Recall constant velocity, closing rates and the momentum equation for one direct impact.
lessons.method:
1. Draw the particles and put the impacts in time order.
  2. Use only the current colliding pair in each momentum calculation.
  3. Carry the resulting velocities forward and recompute the closing rate from the new state.
mistakes: B can have a different velocity at each stage.
Do not reuse the original separation after the second collision.
A particle outside the colliding pair retains its velocity on a smooth line.
lessons.ideas:
For A–B use the two velocities just before and just after that impact. For B–C use the updated velocity of B and the still-current velocity of C.

With B to the left of C and their velocities constant, a positive closing rate gives time \(\frac{\text{B--C gap}}{v_B-v_C}\).

The common final velocity becomes the velocity of the nearer joined body for any later contact test involving A.

Compare the unchanged velocity of A with B’s new velocity just after B meets C. A catches B if \(v_A>v_B\), while both velocities remain fixed.

After finding that gap, divide by the new closing rate to find the time from the second impact to the predicted re-contact.

In a smooth horizontal model the total for A, B and C is the same across both impacts. You still check separation and each subsequent approach separately.

examples.title: Carry the updated velocity to a second impact
examples.question:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest. C is at rest. Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after the B–C impact, C moves to the right at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Give the signed velocity of B after each impact in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(24\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3)(2)+(3)u=24\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

At the second impact the momentum of B and C just before contact is \(18\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3)v+(3)(4)=18\]

B leaves this impact with signed velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The measured velocity of C was \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Calculate the time between the two first impacts
examples.question:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest. C moves to the right at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the first impact the gap between B and C is \(12\,\mathrm m\).

Give the time in seconds from the A–B impact to the B–C impact.
examples.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(20\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(3)+(2)u=20\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

The signed closing rate for B and C is \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Dividing the gap by this rate gives \(2\,\mathrm s\).

examples.title: Calculate the time between the two first impacts
examples.question:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B is at rest. C is at rest. Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At the first impact the gap between B and C is \(12\,\mathrm m\).

Give the time in seconds from the A–B impact to the B–C impact.
examples.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(16\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(2)+(2)u=16\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

The signed closing rate for B and C is \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Dividing the gap by this rate gives \(2\,\mathrm s\).

examples.title: Carry the updated velocity to a second impact
examples.question:
Particles A, B and C have masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) and \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\), in this left-to-right order on a smooth horizontal line. Take rightward as positive. Before the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B moves to the left at \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). C is at rest. Immediately after the A–B impact, A moves to the right at \(\frac{6}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). B and C stick together at their impact.

Give the signed velocity of B after each impact in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
examples.solution:
Conserve momentum for A and B at their impact. Their total is \(15\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(2)(\frac{6}{5})+(3)u=15\]

B leaves this first impact with signed velocity \(\frac{21}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Use it as B’s input to the next stage.

At the second impact conserve momentum for B and C. The pair arrives with total \(\frac{63}{5}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

\[(3+6)v=\frac{63}{5}\]

The joined B–C pair moves with signed velocity \(\frac{7}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

questions.title: Track two momenta through an axis change
questions.prompt_html:
On a straight track, trolley A has mass \(600\,\mathrm g\) and moves to the right at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Trolley B has mass \(\frac{7}{5}\,\mathrm{kg}\) and moves to the left at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Taking rightward as positive, calculate the momentum of A in \(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). [2]

  2. With the same positive direction, find the total momentum of the two trolleys and state its direction. [3]

  3. Repeat the total for leftward positive. State what changes about the physical direction. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(\frac{9}{5}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

  2. \(-1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

    To the left.

  3. \(1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\). The physical direction remains left.

questions.solution_html:

  2. At the second impact the momentum of B and C just before contact is \(12\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\).

    \[(2)v+(4)(3)=12\]

    B leaves this impact with signed velocity \(0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The measured velocity of C was \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

    A still moves to the right with velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so the positive A–B gap closes.

  3. The B–C impact occurs \(2\,\mathrm s\) after the first impact. During that time A and B have separated by \(8\,\mathrm m\).

    The gap now closes at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), so divide the current gap by that rate to obtain \(4\,\mathrm s\).

    Add the two intervals to get \(6\,\mathrm s\).
